prose_changes.old: A continuation of Byzantine Orthodoxy after Constantinople fell in 1453, following on from the earlier fall of Tarnovo, when the patriarch Euthymius went into exile and the Balkan despotate's church carried on. The Patriarchate of Peć was restored in 1557. The controversy around Patriarch Cyril Lucaris — his Greek College ties, his Calvinist-sounding Confession of 1629, his death in 1638, and the church councils that later repudiated his teaching — belongs to the church's own story, not just to the man.
prose_changes.new: The Byzantine church carried on after Constantinople fell in 1453. The fight over Patriarch Cyril Lucaris is part of the church's own story, not just the man's. His enemies included Greeks trained at the Greek College in Rome. His Confession of 1629 sounded like Calvin. He died in 1638, and church councils later condemned his teaching.
prose_changes.reason: Opening reworded as a sentence. Removed the Tarnovo clause and the Pec sentence (no vendored or repo-cited source; the despotate clause was also unclear). 'His Greek College ties' corrected: the Greek College men were Lucaris's opponents (Smith 1707), not his own school. Split for reading level.

prose_changes.old: This is the church that came through. The Ecumenical Patriarchate is still at the Phanar in Istanbul, and the Orthodox churches of Greece, Bulgaria, Serbia and Romania all passed through these centuries. The neomartyrs are commemorated in the Orthodox calendar to this day. The millet arrangement, under which a religious community handled much of its own law and taxation, also shaped the way Balkan national identities later formed around their churches.
prose_changes.new: This is the church that came through. The Ecumenical Patriarchate is still at the Phanar in Istanbul. The Orthodox churches of Greece, Bulgaria, Serbia and Romania all passed through these centuries. The neomartyrs are remembered in the Orthodox calendar to this day. prose_changes.old: It survives as the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church and the Belarusian Greek Catholic Church, and it became the model for the Byzantine-rite unions that followed, one branch of the wider family of Eastern Catholic churches — Eastern in worship, in communion with Rome — that now exists around the world. Suppressed by the Russian Empire in the nineteenth century and again by the Soviet Union in 1946, the Ukrainian church survived underground and re-emerged in 1989 as the largest Eastern Catholic church anywhere.
prose_changes.new: It survives as the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church and the Belarusian Greek Catholic Church. Both belong to the wider family of Eastern Catholic churches around the world. They worship in Eastern ways and are in communion with Rome. The Russian Empire put down the church in the nineteenth century, and the Soviet Union did so again in 1946. The Ukrainian church lived on in secret. It came back in 1989 as the largest Eastern Catholic church anywhere.

prose_changes.old: The Kyiv Mohyla Academy became the leading school of the Orthodox Slavic world and supplied Russia with its educated clergy for a century. One reason Peter the Great's church reforms have a distinctly Kyivan accent. Mohyla's Confession was accepted well beyond Ukraine and remained a standard Orthodox reference text into modern times. The academy itself, closed under Soviet rule, was refounded in 1991 and is now a leading Ukrainian university.
prose_changes.new: The Kyiv Mohyla Academy became the leading school of the Orthodox Slavic world. Moscow drew on its learning. The tsar asked Kyiv for monks from the academy. Later Stephen Yavorsky, sent to Moscow from Kyiv, led the Russian church under Peter the Great. Mohyla's Confession was read far beyond Ukraine. The four Eastern patriarchs approved it in 1643, and it stayed a standard Orthodox guide into modern times. The academy was shut under Soviet rule. It opened again in 1991 and is now one of the best universities in Ukraine.
